notes: Rules: transition = Signal 1 (capitulation) ✓ and close above a rising 200-day MA (rising = higher than 30 days ago); bull market = Signal 1 ✓ and 30 straight closes above a rising 200-day MA, then locked one way; back to bear = 5 straight closes below the 200-day MA during a transition, or 30 straight closes below a falling 200-day MA in a bull market. Supporting signals only show how strong the evidence is and are not part of the call.

Limits: only 3–4 cycles since 2014 can be back-tested. This price rule had the fewest false signals among the candidates, yet it still called a bull market in mid-2019, followed by a drop of nearly 50%; no rule is both fast and low on false signals. A negative 90-day change in exchange supply used to be required, but back-tests showed it fails when the window changes, address attribution is revised after the fact (look-ahead bias), and it held on 99% of days in 2025, so since 2026-10-09 it is only supporting evidence. Bull-market conditions also light up near tops and are not a sell signal; the market stage is only a label and does not drive the exit framework.

rd: #How to read this chart

WhatTop: BTC price; bottom: the weekly regime score (−6 to +6), bars coloured by stage: ≥ +4 overheated (red), the first 26 positive weeks after a real bear early bull (green), other positive bull (amber), negative bear (light blue), ≤ −4 extreme bear (deep blue).

Each is divided by its typical size since 2013 (median), squashed to −1…+1, averaged and multiplied by 6. A flip needs 4 straight weeks on the other side of zero. All inputs are already on the site.

rd: NowHeat 22, Daybreak (early rise), trend bullish.
#How to read this chart

WhatWeekly cycle heat (0–100) around a midline at 50: above 50 it grows up into warm hills (amber, turning red near tops), below 50 down into cool valleys (light blue, turning deep blue near bottoms); the colours are the same stage colours as the weekly regime score. Dots get larger and denser toward the midline. Lines above point to past tops, lines below to past bottoms. Heat ≥ 80 is Dusk, ≤ 10 Deep night; hover for that week's heat, trend and price.

ReadingHeat is valuation, answering "how far from a top or bottom"; trend answers "which way now". Low heat with a bullish flip (Daybreak) has had the best year ahead; high heat (Dusk) has been roughly flat a year later, with close to even odds of a fall.
CaveatIn the last two cycles valuations peaked before price, so Dusk tends to come early; with only three-plus full cycles the stats describe history and are not a signal.
notes: A cycle seen as a day: Deep night (bottom zone) → Daybreak (early rise) → Daylight (rising) → Dusk (overheated) → Nightfall (falling). Heat = the average percentile, against the past 4 years, of LTH NUPL, unrealized profit ÷ market cap, the power-law residual, reserve risk and MVRV-Z; trend = price ÷ 200-day MA, price ÷ STH cost basis, 30-day aSOPR and the 90-day realized profit ÷ loss, flipping after 4 straight weeks. Stages: heat ≥ 80 Dusk, ≤ 10 Deep night; otherwise bearish = Nightfall, bullish with heat < 50 = Daybreak, else Daylight. Every week uses only data available then (no look-ahead). In research its rank correlation with the hindsight cycle position was 0.82 (weekly regime score: 0.49). Data: Bitview, CoinMetrics, CheckOnChain. Only three-plus full cycles; the table describes history and is not a trading signal.

Since 2012, stretches below 1 lasting 10+ days: a year later 5 of 10 rose, median +60.9% (any day: 71% rose, median +85.3%). Recent: 2018/05/22–2019/05/09 (345 days, 1y -4%), 2019/11/21–2020/01/06 (47 days, 1y +145%), 2020/03/09–2020/04/25 (48 days, 1y +593%), 2022/05/06–2023/06/20 (396 days, 1y -20%), 2023/07/24–2023/10/20 (88 days, 1y +126%). rd: NowAVIV 0.948 (below 1 for 6 days).
#How to read this chart
WhatAVIV = price ÷ the true market mean (log scale); teal shading is below 1, capsules the past tops and bottoms.
ReadingAbove 1 = active investors in profit, higher means closer to overheating; below 1 = active investors at a loss, where bear markets mostly sit. Tops fall and bottoms rise each cycle.
CaveatThe true market mean is a modelled cost of active capital (Cointime), different from the ordinary realized price.
notes: AVIV = price ÷ the true market mean (the average cost of active capital only, excluding long-dormant and lost coins; Cointime, via Bitview). At 1, price sits exactly at active investors' average cost. Log scale. Reading only.

title: Reserve risk

items.d: Reserve risk 1.17‰, the 19th percentile of the last 4 years (8th of all history); the low zone (bottom 10% of 4 years) now starts below 1.08‰. Tops fall each cycle — 2013 38.47‰, 2017 31.45‰, 2021 5.63‰, 2025 2.58‰ — while bottoms stay around 0.8–1.6‰, flattening the series, so an all-history percentile leans toward recent years; this uses the last 4 years.
Each bear-market bottom against its own previous 4 years: 2015/01 0th, 2018/12 26th, 2022/11 0th, 2026/06 6th. The late-2018 bottom only reached the 26th, so this gauge alone can miss a bottom.

Stretches at or below the 10th percentile of 4 years: 6 (4 since 2022); of the 4 with a full year since, 2 were higher a year later: 2014/09/18 (375 days, 1y -45%), 2020/03/12 (45 days, 1y +1056%), 2022/05/09 (270 days, 1y -9%), 2023/09/01 (13 days, 1y +129%). Few cases with mixed results; reading only.

rd: Now1.17‰ (19th percentile of 4 years).
#How to read this chart
WhatReserve risk (log scale, per mille); the teal dashed line is the rolling 4-year bottom-10% threshold, the amber one the top 10%; teal shading marks time in the low zone.
ReadingLow = price is cheap relative to long-term holder conviction, historically near bear-market bottoms; high = price running ahead of conviction, the top zone.

title: Capital efficiency by cycle

items.d: From each bear-market bottom to the top, money in: $2.90B → $70.0B → $366B → $698B; price multiple: 539× → 112× → 21× → 7.9×. More money each cycle, smaller gains each cycle: the bigger the market, the more money the same gain takes.

132 days from the 2026/06/30 bottom: +$20.4B in, price 1.28×. Past cycles on the same day: the 2011 cycle $0M, 2.28×; the 2015 cycle -$200M, 1.35×; the 2018 cycle -$3.10B, 1.62×; the 2022 cycle -$7.80B, 1.78×. More money in than past cycles at this point, yet a smaller gain.
By the top, each $1 of inflow added $4.8 → $4.7 → $3.3 → $3.1 of market cap. This cycle is young and inflows are small, so the ratio only means something later in the cycle.

rd: NowThis cycle, 132 days: +$20.4B in, 1.28×.
#How to read this chart

WhatEach row is one cycle from bear-market bottom to top: teal is the money that came in (realized cap added), gold the price multiple, with logarithmic bar lengths; the last row is this cycle so far.

ReadingThe bigger bitcoin gets, the more money the same gain needs: inflows grow each cycle while multiples shrink. Comparing this cycle with past ones on the same day shows how fast money arrives and how price responds.
CaveatBottom and top dates follow this site's cycle model; realized cap is per UTXO and affected by exchange reshuffles and lost coins, so read it for orders of magnitude.
notes: Realized cap = every coin valued at the price it last moved; its increase is the money that actually came in (market cap ÷ MVRV, CoinMetrics). Each cycle runs from the bear-market bottom to the cycle top; bar lengths are logarithmic. "Market cap per $1 in" = market cap added ÷ realized cap added. Bottom and top dates follow this site's cycle model. Reading only.

title: Power law: price ÷ fair value
src: Fitted daily using only data up to that day
says: Now 0.52× (fair value $145,503, 48% below trend). Top multiples shrink every cycle; at this rate the next top would be around 0.40–0.87× fair value. Price is 52% of the power-law fair value ($145,503), 48% below trend: below fair value but above the historical bottom band (0.48×) — cheap-ish on a long-term view. Channel position 10% (Bottom zone): 0% is the line through past bottoms, 100% the falling line through past tops; past tops sat at 78–100%, bottoms at 0–14%.
rd: #How to read this chart

WhatTop: BTC price and the power-law fair value (grey dashes); the channel view also draws the top line (red dashes) and bottom line (blue dashes). Bottom, two views. Channel: 0% is the line through past bottoms, 100% the line through past tops (falling each cycle); the line is coloured in five stages: bottom zone < 15%, low, middle, high, top zone ≥ 75%. Multiple: price divided by the power-law fair value (log scale); the blue band is the historical bottom zone, red dots tops, blue dots bottoms.
ReadingThe channel builds in the shrinking tops: every past top sat above 75% and every bottom below 15%. Higher multiples mean more expensive.
CaveatThe power law uses only data up to each day, but the channel edges are fitted through all four tops and bottoms, so the history is drawn after the fact, from only four cycles. Read-only.

title: Short-term holder profit-taking and capitulation spikes

items.d: Capitulation spike: profit-taking -0.9, capitulation 2.7 (-0.5 and 3.1 a week ago); over the last 5 days short-term holders realized about $116M of profit and $393M of loss a day. Short-term holders are selling at a loss far more than usual for the past three and a half months, day 1 so far. That is panic selling, but in the past it did not mean the drop was over (see the backtest below).

Each line is compared with its own last 105 days. A high profit-taking reading means short-term holders are selling at a gain far more than usual, which follows sharp rallies; a high capitulation reading means they are selling at a loss far more than usual, which comes with sharp drops (drawn as negative). Above 2 counts as a spike and is shaded. It measures "unusual versus recent", not size: after a long quiet stretch a little selling triggers it, while right after a big drop the same amount does not.

Since 2012, 64 times (14+ days apart). 30 days later: 34 of 63 rose, median +1.9% (any day: 57% rose, median +3.1%); 90 days later: 36 of 63 rose, median +10.9% (any day: 60% rose, median +10.2%). No different from buying on any day: a capitulation spike is not a low-risk entry. Of the 23 below the 200-day average, only 10 were higher 30 days later. Recent examples: 1/23, -25% over the next 30 days; 5/29, -19% over the next 30 days.

Since 2012, 57 times. 90 days later: 34 of 54 rose, median +13.4% (any day: 60% rose, median +10.2%). Not a sell signal overall; position matters. With the close above the 200-day average, 27 of 31 rose, median +35.1% (any day: 67% rose, median +19.0%), mostly continuation; below it, 7 of 23 rose, median -8.3% (any day: 48% rose, median -2.2%), a rally in a downtrend being sold into. The close is now above the 200-day average ($73,137).

Profit-taking spikes: 2/6 (-6%), 3/4 (-8%), 4/11 (+12%), 8/19 (+17%), 9/21 (-3%), 10/22. Capitulation spikes: 1/23 (-25%), 5/29 (-19%), 6/26 (+9%), 7/13 (+2%), 10/30. Brackets show the next 30 days; not listed until 30 days have passed.

#How to read this chart

WhatTwo lines below: green is the profit-taking reading (upward), red the capitulation reading (drawn negative, downward); the dashed lines are the ±2 threshold. Periods beyond it are shaded green or red, and capsules give each period's peak.

ReadingGreen shading = short-term holders taking profit in a burst: above the 200-day average it has mostly meant continuation, below it a rally being sold into. Red shading = a burst of loss selling: panic, but returns afterward look like any other day, so it does not mean the drop is over.
CaveatIt measures how unusual today is against its own last 105 days, not size; per-UTXO data, so exchange wallet reshuffles can cause one-day spikes. A reading, not a trade signal.
notes: Ours, from Bitview data (per UTXO, not entity-adjusted). It takes the profit and the loss realized each day on coins held under 6 months (USD), divides each by the short-term holder realized cap (that group's total cost), smooths with a 5-day exponential average, then scores it against its own last 105 days: (today − 105-day mean) ÷ 105-day standard deviation. The age bands run to 6 months, slightly past the 155-day short-term holder cut-off. Exchange and custody wallet reshuffles also register as realized profit or loss, so a one-day spike is not necessarily trading. The parameters were picked against 2026 price action; 90 or 120 days give the same conclusions with dates shifting by a few days. Reading only, not a trade signal.

WhatTop: BTC price, the average cost of coins short-term holders sold over 7 days (purple) and the cost of those still holding (orange). Bottom: the gap between the two ÷ close; green ≥ +0.05, red ≤ −0.05, the yellow band is the transition zone.

#How to read this chart

WhatTop: BTC price with a bubble for each day's net realized profit/loss (green = net profit selling, red = net loss selling, bigger = larger, thick ring = most extreme 2% of the prior year); bottom: the same numbers as daily bars. Switch to “30-day total” for the cycle view: the bottom pane is the 30-day total as % of market cap, the red line minus a quarter of the prior 4 years' largest 30-day net profit, and orange rings the first breaches.

ReadingBig green bubbles cluster on rallies and highs: profit taking; shrinking green bubbles mean fewer holders want to sell at this price. Big red bubbles on pullbacks are loss capitulation, which does not mean the low is in.

CaveatNet only (profit minus loss), so the two sides are not visible separately; exchange-internal transfers also realize P/L. In tests since 2015 using only data known on the day, loss spikes were followed by ordinary returns (not a buy signal), and profit spikes were more often followed by further gains, weaker each cycle (not a sell signal). First breaches of the 30-day red line since 2015: 2015/01, 2018/11, 2020/03, 2022/05, 2022/11, 2026/02, 2026/06; 4 of the 5 before 2023 were higher a year later (2022/05 was −7%), and after 2018/11 and 2022/05 price still fell another 26% and 46%. After March 2028 the 2024/3 profit peak leaves the 4-year window and the line will rise to about −1%. The signal may be blunter in the ETF era: ETF shares changing hands on the stock market do not move coins on-chain, only net redemptions do; this cycle's deepest loss was only 30–40% of its largest profit, versus about 70% in the previous two.
notes: Method: the daily change in realized cap (market cap ÷ MVRV) minus newly mined coins equals the net of “sale price − last-moved price” for coins moved that day; it matches Glassnode's Net Realized Profit/Loss in direction and size. Net only; in daily mode a thick ring marks the most extreme 2% of the prior year; the 30-day mode is shown as % of market cap, and the red line is minus a quarter of the largest 30-day net profit of the prior 4 years (computed day by day from data known at the time). #How to read this chart

What$2,000 buckets: short-term holders (held under 155 days) on the left, long-term holders on the right, the line is the close; the shaded band is the range price covered in the past 155 days. Switch to “STH change / LTH change” to compare with about 30 days ago: grey is then, colour is now.

ReadingShort-term holders piled above the close are underwater and tend to sell when price returns to their cost; piled below, they stay in profit until price falls back, the first layer of support. Long-term holder piles move slowly; a shrinking bucket means long-term holders with that cost are selling.

Caveat“Now” is CheckOnChain's actual coin-age data (falls back to the estimate if unavailable); “changes” are estimated. Both are per-UTXO, not entity-adjusted, so exchange wallet reshuffles look like selling and rebuying (large, concentrated one-day moves are put back at their original cost). Outside the shaded band there are only long-term holders.
notes: “Now” comes from CheckOnChain's public chart (Bitcoin Research Kit, using each coin's actual age), regrouped into $2,000 buckets. “30 days ago” comes from Bitview (the public API of the same Bitcoin Research Kit) with the same transfer correction, so the STH/LTH change views compare actual with actual; only who sold and who aged into long-term (the flows below) is still estimated. How changes are estimated: coins created each day go into the buckets that day's price range covered; then age-band and price-bucket totals are matched to bitcoin-data's HODL waves and URPD at the same time. Held under 155 days = short-term holder. Price covered 57.7K–87.4K in the past 155 days; outside that range there are only long-term holders, no model involved; inside it the split is an estimate. Per-UTXO, not entity-adjusted like Glassnode: exchange and custodian wallet reshuffles look like selling and rebuying, so turnover reads high; large one-day moves from buckets far from the price into the current price (likely one entity moving its own coins) are put back at their original cost and age.

title: Price × long-term holder flow

items.d: Long-term holders have been net sellers for 98 days since 8/4 while price moved +18%, and the LTH ÷ STH supply ratio fell from a 1-year high of 5.32 to 4.25: supply is passing from long-term holders to short-term holders, and it is being absorbed (price has not fallen). Every past climb from the true market mean to a new high needed this handover, and it always took a while; we read it as mid-cycle digestion, not top distribution.

items.d: Net reducing for 98 straight days since 8/4 (peak −265K BTC), while price moved +18% ($64,054 → $75,253): price up while long-term holders cut, so they are selling into the rally and supplying the market above.

Long-term 16,280K BTC ÷ short-term 3,830K BTC (Bitview, 11/10). 30 days ago 4.54 (-6.4%), a year ago 3.11; 1-year high 5.32 (2026/07/27), low 2.40 (2025/12/10); 91th percentile since 2015. Falling = more short-term supply (long-term holders distributing or short-term holders arriving); rising = supply settling (including coins simply aging past 155 days).

0 = the heaviest net reduction in four years, 100 = the heaviest net addition. Before this run, the last time it was this negative was 2025/12/21 (−108K BTC, price $88,622). Price is 29% below the one-year high of $105,973.

rd: #How to read this chart
WhatBTC price on a log scale, coloured by long-term holders' (held 155+ days) net change over 30 days: red = net cut, grey = flat, green = net add, deepest at ±400K BTC.

ReadingRed at high prices means long-term holders selling into strength (as in Mar 2024, late 2024 and Sep–Nov 2025); turning green after a drop means long-term holders are holding and supply is settling. Price rising on a red line means the rally is being met with supply.
CaveatGreen is not buying: coins become long-term automatically at 155 days. Grouped by coin age with exchanges included; Glassnode's Accumulation Trend Score is entity-based and a different metric.
notes: Long-term holder = held 155 days or more. A rising net position is not all buying: coins become “long-term” automatically once they reach 155 days. This is not Glassnode's Accumulation Trend Score (entity-based, exchanges excluded, paid data); bitcoin-data's indicator of that name is a rescaling of this same series.

#How to read this chart

What30-day change of long- ÷ short-term holder supply: orange (negative) = long-term holder coins passing to short-term holders, teal (positive) = supply settling. Pale amber shading is the year before each cycle top (the main up-leg), pale blue the year after each bear-market bottom (the transition); the shares in the readings above count negative days inside these windows.
ReadingMain up-legs are mostly negative — long-term holders sell and new demand absorbs it; many negative days in a transition mean strong demand, an even split goes with flatter prices.

title: Short-term holder supply, 90-day change

items.d: Short-term holder supply is 3.83M BTC versus 3.42M 90 days ago. Positive since 2026/09/05; this run's high was +542K on 2026/10/23, 134K lower since; 30 days ago it was +433K.

Positive = more coins were moved in the past 90 days (and so count as short-term) than aged past 155 days into long-term: long-term holders selling to new buyers, plus exchange or custody wallet moves. Negative = coins sitting still and aging into long-term. It measures whether coins move, not directly whether short-term holders are buying or selling.

The largest reading within six months of each top: 2014/01 +1.61M, 2017/09 +1.75M, 2022/03 +291K, 2025/11 +1.54M. Now +408K. The 2021 cycle is unusually small because its big turnover came earlier, in late 2020 to early 2021.

Since 2015 it turned positive 13 times; 90 days later 9 of 13 rose, median +13.5% (any day: 60% rose, median +9.4%). It turned negative 14 times; 11 rose, median +12.9%. A flip on its own is not a buy or sell signal.

rd: Now90-day +408K BTC.
#How to read this chart

WhatBottom: short-term holder supply minus its level 90 days earlier; orange = rising (more coins moved into short-term hands than aged into long-term), teal = falling (coins settling). Capsules mark the largest reading around each top.

ReadingStrongly positive = heavy turnover of old coins, typical of late-bull distribution by long-term holders or of old coins sold in a panic; turning negative = newly bought coins sitting still as supply settles.
CaveatIt counts coin movement, not who is buying; exchange and custody reshuffles are included. Returns 90 days after a flip look like any other day, so a flip is not a trading signal.
notes: Short-term holders = coins held under 155 days (since their last move; per UTXO, not entity-adjusted). Value = today's short-term holder supply minus 90 days earlier, from Bitview, plotted every 3 days. Exchange and custody wallet reshuffles also make coins "younger", so a jump is not necessarily trading. Reading only.

#How to read this chart
WhatPurple is 7-day dormancy, orange the 30-day average (log scale); capsules mark the highs near cycle tops.
ReadingHigh = coins spent had been held a long time, old coins moving; low for a long stretch = only young coins selling, old coins quiet, often near bottoms.

title: Long-term holder supply in loss

items.d: 34.8% of coins held 155+ days cost more than today's price. This cycle's peak was 45.4% (2026/06/30, price $58,367), the low since 26.0% (2026/10/04); now up 8.8 points.

From today's long-term holder supply map (CheckOnChain, 11/10), a drop to about $61,000 would push the share above this cycle's 45.4% peak, breaking the “no new high after the bottom” pattern; at 68K it would be about 39%. Recent high-priced buyers turn long-term after 155 days, so the line drifts up if price stalls; it is recomputed daily.

Peaks at bear-market bottoms: 2015/08 53.0%, 2019/03 46.4%, 2022/12 44.7%, 2026/06 45.4%. In earlier cycles it never made a new high after leaving the bottom: after 2015 the max was 36.7% (2015/11), after 2019 the max was 42.5% (2020/03), after 2022 the max was 32.6% (2023/03). Only 3–4 cycles; 2015's 53% peak was also higher than later ones.

This cycle's largest long-term holder capitulation was only 0.29% (2026/06); past bear-market bottoms reached at least 0.86%. Two readings: this cycle fell less (deepest -53% vs −77% to −85% before) and never needed a mass capitulation, or the real one is still ahead. We lean to the first: long-term holders' share in loss peaked at 45.4% in 2026/06, inside the 42–48% band of past bottoms, consistent with this cycle's low already being in. The last 7 days at 0.09% (71th percentile) show some long-term holders still selling at a loss near current prices, so the overhang is not fully cleared.

items.d: Over the past 7 days long-term holders realized about $1.4B of losses selling below cost, 0.09% of market cap (11/10); 71th percentile since 2015.

Largest in past bear markets: 2015/01 0.86%, 2018/12 2.86%, 2022/06 1.34%. In 2018 the loss shrank from June to August to October and the biggest capitulation still came after, so “a new low with a smaller loss” is not on its own a sign of seller exhaustion.

#How to read this chart
WhatTop: BTC price; bottom: the share of long-term holder (155+ days) supply at a loss. Red circles mark peaks at past bear-market bottoms, the red band is 42–48%, the dashed line this cycle's peak.

ReadingIt peaks at bear-market bottoms (2019, 2022 and 2026 all at 42–48%); after leaving the bottom, earlier cycles never made a new high, and its rebounds (price pullbacks) were often early-bull buying windows. A move above the dashed line would break that pattern.
CaveatNot price alone: recent high-priced buyers become long-term holders after 155 days, which lifts the share even if price stalls. Only 3–4 cycles, and a pattern seen in hindsight.
notes: The share of coins held 155+ days (long-term holders) whose cost is above the current price. At bear-market bottoms many long-term holders are underwater and it peaks; it falls as price recovers. Data from CheckOnChain (Bitcoin Research Kit, by each coin's actual age). Source chart ↗

Losses long-term holders (155+ days) realize when selling below their own cost, summed over 7 days and divided by market cap so years compare. Data from Bitview (per UTXO, not Glassnode's entity-adjusted version, so self-transfers can count). A swing low is a close that is the lowest within 30 days either side and 20%+ below the prior 180-day high.

title: Sell Pressure Index and momentum quality

items.d: Bottom combo on: pressure 100 (80 a week ago; rising from 0 since 10/7), momentum quality 0.20 (0.23 a week ago). Both conditions hold: pressure at 100 (day 1) and momentum below 0.3. Weakness has dragged on and the drop is still fast and steady; in the past this often came late in a decline, though another leg down was common first. Relative unrealized profit is 36.7%, at or below 37.5%: the group with the better record (see "Near the floor or not").

Since 2012, 20 times (60+ days apart). 30 days later: 11 of 20 rose, median +1.8% (any day: 57% rose, median +3.2%); 90 days later: 12 of 20 rose, median +17.8% (any day: 60% rose, median +9.9%). Another leg down was common in the short run; three months on the median beat a random day, but the share of gains was about the same.

On the day the combo appears, also read relative unrealized profit (unrealized profit ÷ market cap). At or below 37.5% (8 times): 90 days later 6 of 7 rose, median +25.0%; exiting when pressure resets, 7 of 7 won, median +10.9%, median further dip -8.1%. Above 37.5% (13 times): 90 days later 6 of 13 rose, median -7.3%; exit, 8 of 13 won, median +1.8%, median further dip -20.9%. Counting every day with pressure at 100: 96 days at or below 37.5%, 100% higher a year later, median +105%; 233 days above it, only 37% higher a year later, median -19% (any day: 70%, +78%). Pressure at 100 only says the short-term drop has run long; how close the cycle floor is comes from relative unrealized profit. Pressure also reaches 100 early in bear markets, when relative unrealized profit is usually still above 37.5%. Few cases; a reading only.

Buy when the combo appears, sell when pressure returns to 0: 15 of 20 won, median +8.0% over a median 76 days, with a median further dip of -12.2% along the way. By era: 2012–17 4/6, 2018–22 5/8, 2023–26 6/6. The worst ones mostly came early in bear markets: 2014/08 -42%, 2022/05 -34%, 2018/01 -3%, 2021/12 -2%. The latest, 2026/11/10, has not reset yet.

items.k: Strong momentum is not a top
items.d: Of 24 times with pressure 0 and momentum above 0.85 (a fast, steady rise), 14 were higher 90 days later, median +25.7%: usually continuation; only bear-market rallies tended to peak here.

rd: NowPressure 100, momentum 0.20.
#How to read this chart

WhatBottom: the red line is the Sell Pressure Index (0–100), the teal line momentum quality (0–1, drawn on the same height, 0.3 at 30). Teal shading runs from each bottom combo to when pressure returns to 0; capsules show the next 90 days.

ReadingMomentum quality asks whether the last 21 days moved fast and steadily; the Sell Pressure Index asks how long weakness has dragged on. A one- or two-day drop does not push it to 100 — weakness has to linger — and a fast, steady rally clears it. When both hit extremes (pressure 100, momentum < 0.3), it has tended to come late in a decline, though often with another leg down first.
CaveatPrice only, no on-chain data; about twenty cases, and it failed repeatedly early in bear markets. High momentum is not a top signal: it usually meant continuation.
notes: Ours, from daily closes only. Momentum quality = mean ÷ standard deviation of the last 21 daily returns × √21, mapped to 0–1 with the normal distribution: near 1 for a fast, steady rise, near 0 for a fast, steady fall. The Sell Pressure Index is half a slow line and half a fast one. The slow line runs on a second, shorter momentum: the exponentially weighted mean ÷ standard deviation of daily returns (span 10 days, recent days weigh more), mapped to 0–1 the same way. It adds up each day that sits below 0.45 (more the further below) and drains at the same rate when above. The fast line uses the 5-day average of each day’s move ÷ the 30-day volatility: it adds when that average is negative and drains when positive, so a big down day moves it at once. Both are capped at 0–100 and a bounce pulls them back the same day; pressure reads 100 only when both lines are there, so a one- or two-day drop does not take it to 100. Bottom combo = pressure 100 and momentum quality below 0.3. The backtest has only about twenty cases; a different close source or a small parameter change shifts the counts by a few. Since 2026-11-11 the index is calculated this way (it used the 21-day momentum and reset to zero at 0.7 before), and the history was recalculated. Reading only, not a trade signal.
